title: Diamonds lose Commonwealth Games semifinal

Topic:Commonwealth Games

Sun 2 Aug 2026 at 4:55am

The usually clinical Diamonds missed out in the crucial moments. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

When Sophie Dwyer's shot bounced off the front right of the rim, the first look on her face was shock.

As she turned and was dragged into something vaguely resembling a hug by veteran centre Kate Moloney, Dwyer's thousand-mile stare was one of numbness and utter disbelief.

Australia had lost its semifinal to Jamaica by 46-45 and would miss the Commonwealth Games gold medal match for the first time in history.

The Diamonds certainly did not expect to lose this game, they never do, but when they were down by four with four minutes left, they probably did not expect to be shooting for extra time with the clock at 00:00 either.

Moloney was at pains to point out how much went wrong before Dwyer, the second youngest member of the team, had to take a long shot to tie the game, rushing through the moment in an apparent attempt to give nerves no chance to set in.

"It's a full team loss today, it's not on one person," she said.

The Diamonds were this close to potentially saving themselves from disaster. (Reuters: Andrew Couldridge)

It had been their worst performance of an otherwise cruisy tournament, culminating in a final quarter that started 35-35 but quickly ballooned out on the back of miscommunication with the ball in hand, leading to uncharacteristic and costly late turnovers.

To focus solely on Australia's errors would do a disservice to the Sunshine Girls' harrying defence, but Moloney admitted her usually nerveless Diamonds were nowhere near their best.

"We have the players to get the job done, but we just didn't do it today," she said.

Things turned frantic in the final quarter. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"We just couldn't execute at really critical moments, and that's really important. It's something we speak about all the time and there's a few errors I'm sure we wish we could go back and take again.

"Credit to Jamaica, but we needed to be better today."

In an Australian team full of expected gold medals, the netball felt like one of the most secure after four victories from seven straight finals.

We saw Nina Kennedy unable to live up to similarly lofty expectations, but fans were never actively rooting against her success.

Nina Kennedy can measure success in a lot of different ways, and it wasn't necessarily in metres or centimetres in Glasgow.

Every one of the Diamonds' opponents became de facto hometown favourites at the Hydro, and it was again the case in their semi.

Moloney said they were used to having the crowd rooting against their success, in an apparent acknowledgement that it would mostly likely come regardless, but the support for Jamaica felt different.

Once it became clear that they might be able to not just make the presumptive and defending champions bleed a little, but actually take them down, the tone turned as much anti-Australia as it was pro-Jamaica.

Taking down the Australian giants guaranteed the Sunshine GIrls at least a silver medal. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

"We don't really notice that, we're pretty used to that," Moloney said.

"I think there were just critical moments today that we weren't able to nail."

And that didn't just start when the game was at its most tense.

Although coach Stacey Marinkovich ran her best seven, the Diamonds got off to a slow start.

With an almost entirely Melbourne Vixens' frontline, there was a clear mental hangover from the Super Netball grand final.

Sophie Garbin, Kiera Austin and Moloney were all part of the side that lost to the Adelaide Thunderbirds by a record margin in that decider, 61-40.

So it was no real surprise that once again, the very next time they met, Jamaican defenders Shamera Sterling-Humphrey and Latanya Wilson had them spooked.

All had been running smoothly in the pool stages with the team winning comprehensively by margins of 61, 19, 36, 10 and 61 goals.

But in the semifinal the attackers were stuck in their heads, second-guessing their connections and making rushed decisions that led to turnover.

Australia went down 13-10 at the first break and the margin got as big as five in the second period. They were on the back foot.

Maybe this failure to address these demons ahead of the Games will come back to bite Marinkovich? As might her changes in live play.

The first substitution of the night to bring Cara Koenen on in goal shooter was the right call. Koenen helped Australia win gold in Birmingham and despite only averaging about 25 minutes of play before the finals, her experience meant she was very much ready to go.

The defence by Shamera Sterling-Humphrey and Latanya Wilson was stifling. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

With Koenen involved for 44 minutes, the Australians ground their way into the contest and managed to win the second and third quarters.

Koenen was so close to being the hero — turning herself inside out to make rushed and misplaced passes look good, trusting her hold and take when she was sandwiched by the defenders. She was steady and reliable under the post with 18 goals at 90 per cent.

The struggles continued at the other end of the court where Courtney Bruce, who has had a strong hold on the starting goal keeper bib, caught the eye of the umpires early and was often standing out of play.

Bruce did come up with a couple of crucial gains to help the team get back in contention, but her overall impact was limited due to so much whistle.

The highest penalised player on court (14 contacts, five obstructions) struggled to get off the body of goal-shooter Romelda Aiken-George, but she wasn't alone as Sarah Klau, Matilda Garrett and Jo Weston could not find a way to shut down Jamaican linchpin Shanice Beckford. They really needed to invest more of their time planning tactics in this area.

At the final break, the score was level 35-35.

For the first time in this campaign, Georgie Horjus was left on the bench all game. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Austin had been left on and managed to toil away alongside Koenen. By now fans were confident she could pull the side through. But midway through the final term, with just seven minutes to play, Marinkovich pulled Austin off and injected Dwyer.

We had seen this change throughout the pool stages when the Diamonds were up by much safer margins, but the Dwyer-Koenen partnership was very much untested against Sterling-Humphrey, and it was a huge risk in a match of this nature.

Dwyer had a very difficult season with the Giants, winning just one game all year. Her confidence is not at its peak and to come on cold like this and execute was a huge ask that she came within a missed shot of answering.

It was a huge call from Marinkovich at a crucial point Australia's first-ever Commonwealth Games semifinal loss. Less damaging decisions have cost other coaches more, and Marinkovich's contract is up after next year's World Cup, where the expectations will now be even greater than they were in Glasgow.

If the Diamonds were not going to stick with Austin, then Georgie Horjus at least deserved a crack. Bizarrely, the country's most in-form domestic talent — off the back of winning a third Super Netball premiership, training alongside the Jamaican defenders in Adelaide for several years — was the only player that did not hit the court in this semifinal.

This is not on Dwyer missing the final shot. This call is on the coaching staff.

How could it all go so wrong?
